title: Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed makes a play for RFK Jr.'s MAHA voters
description:
Washington — Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed is making a play for Robert F. Kennedy Jr.'s "Make America Healthy Again" supporters with the release Tuesday of a new health policy platform.
"I think we have an opportunity to remind folks that we've always been the people who want people to be healthier, rather than the folks who capitulate to the food, ag and pharmaceutical corporations that are too often on the wrong side of things," El-Sayed told CBS News. 
The platform, dubbed the Building A Healthier America Policy Agenda, takes aim at pesticides in food, backing legislation that would give people the right to sue pesticide manufacturers over harm caused by the products.

fullText:
President Donald Trump has personally driven the controversial, taxpayer-funded video ads promoting himself and his administration’s policies, including helping select the imagery and videos used, a source familiar with the matter told CNN.

Two Trump advisers familiar with the ads said that they were being created in-house by the White House video team — which is part of the communications team, responsible for the administration’s public messaging.

Coming just over a month before the November midterms, the ads have generated bipartisan criticism over how the Trump administration is spending taxpayer dollars.

“It’s a great message. I like the message, but it shouldn’t be paid for with taxpayer dollars,” Senate Majority Leader John Thune told reporters in the Capitol on Monday.

GOP Sen. John Cornyn of Texas echoed that sentiment: “It’s not even a close question.”

The White House has broadly defended the ads, saying they are akin to public service announcements past administrations have put out about Medicare, Obamacare and Covid-19 vaccinations. Officials have insisted they “are very clearly not campaign ads.”

“These public service announcements are about reminding Americans to love their country and understand what makes it worth defending, at home, at our borders, and abroad,” a White House spokesperson said Monday.

But the imagery is undeniably meant to promote Trump, casting him as a warrior battling against existential threats. And the latest one appears nearly identical to a video Trump posted on Truth Social in January 2024, during his third presidential campaign.

That most recent ad shows Trump walking down a hall as audio plays of him saying “this is the final battle.”

“We will cast out the communists, Marxists and fascists. We will throw off the sick political class that hates our country. We will rout the fake news media, and we will liberate America from these villains once and for all,” Trump says in the ad, echoing comments he made during a Veterans Day speech in 2023.

The version on Truth Social has an additional six seconds that includes Trump’s campaign logo and a number to text. The text “Paid for by the US Government” is seen across the screen at the end of the new version of the ad.

Multiple members of Trump’s political operation said they were unaware that these ads were coming until they aired. But another source pushed back on the notion that anyone was kept in the dark — noting that the president had spoken about the ads to multiple aides and advisers and insisting that they were not being made in secret.

The latest ad — which aired during at least two NFL games on Sunday, during Fox’s broadcasts of the Washington Commanders-Seattle Seahawks matchup as well as the Carolina Panthers-Cleveland Browns game — is the third government-funded message in recent days to be captured by the media tracker AdImpact.

An ad that began airing Wednesday featured rapidly edited pictures and video of Trump over audio of him denouncing communism and socialism. Text on the screen touted his administration’s accomplishments, including “reigniting American manufacturing.”

“The ad is educational and unapologetically patriotic,” a White House spokesperson said in a statement. “We should be proud of our country.”

The music used in that ad — a song called “Love Me” by JMSN — has also come under scrutiny. Lawyers for the artist sent White House chief of staff Susie Wiles a letter on Monday asking the administration to “immediately withdraw the advertisement from all scheduled airings” and “cease and desist any use of the Song and/or any of the intellectual property of JMSN.”

A second ad features video of Trump at Mount Rushmore as his voice is heard saying, “Never before has any nation celebrated so magnificent a triumph as this one.”

Beyond questions of intellectual property, watchdog groups say the ads mark a clear violation of appropriations law restricting the use of federal funding for propaganda or partisan communications.

“The most immediate check on this kind of behavior is supposed to be and needs to be Congress. Congress has not asserted itself as the first branch of government with the power of the purse to hold the president accountable,” said Donald Sherman, president and CEO of Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics, or CREW, in Washington.

GOP lawmakers may be hesitant to provide accountability, he added, because the ads “are designed to boost Republicans in Congress,” he said.

And, Sherman noted, the Government Accountability Office — the nonpartisan agency that would be tasked with investigations into this type of issue — is currently without Senate-confirmed leadership.

“That makes it that much harder for them to move with speed to address a high-profile and politically sensitive investigation like this requires,” he said.

Democratic Rep. Jamie Raskin, the ranking member of the House Judiciary Committee, said in a post on X that the ads “may be felony criminal theft and conversion of government property for political campaign purposes.”

And Raskin, who will gain congressional subpoena power in November if Democrats win the House, said it is not just Trump who might face inquiries over the messages. He said the creation of the ads was a “Hatch Act violation for any government employees who worked on it or used government resources to make it.”

“This is dumb, dumb, dumb beyond belief,” one former Trump campaign official told CNN. “These guys are all gonna get subpoenaed. It’s gonna be bad.”

The story has been updated with additional information.

CNN’s Kit Maher contributed to this report.

fullText:
President Trump gathered top artificial intelligence leaders in Washington on Tuesday and doubled down on his opposition to government intervention, suggesting that "self-regulation" is the answer to growing worries about the technology getting out of human control.

"There's a belief that there should be tremendous self-regulation," the president said after meeting with the assembled CEOs. "There was a lot of commonality in this room."

Trump said he and the CEOs signed a "morally binding" accord that wasn't immediately released but that the president said would keep the companies in line through "self-policing and group policing."

Some executives on hand said the so-called Accord on Super Intelligence would include commitments to a combination of technological controls to detect problems with new models, internal risk review efforts, external auditors, and other measures.

Meta (META) CEO Mark Zuckerberg called the accord "a start," while others suggested some details still needed to be worked out.

"The mechanism, how we address those risks, is still under discussion," Anthropic (ANTH.PVT) CEO Dario Amodei said. Progress had been made toward both the US winning AI and also winning safely, he said, though he emphasized that the technology still poses "real dangers."

Amodei published an essay earlier this month titled "We Must Pace the Frontier," which set off a fierce debate about the need for a cooperative slowdown in AI capability.

The accord also formally changed the name of the technology in government record-keeping to Super Intelligence.

"We've changed the name officially to SI," Trump said.

The "meeting and luncheon on Super Intelligence," as the White House described the event, took place in the East Room, with Trump even posting the seating chart. The location was the same spot where just a few days ago, many of the same AI leaders gathered for a state dinner for Chinese President Xi Jinping.

Elon Musk of Tesla (TSLA), Jensen Huang of Nvidia (NVDA), and Lisa Su of Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) were all at the head table with Xi last Thursday and again received prominent spots near Trump.

After the meeting, Trump also said he was "very close" to a decision on an AI czar and would announce it in the next three to four days.

Other notable guests included Google (GOOGL, GOOG) CEO Sundar Pichai, Microsoft (MSFT) CEO Satya Nadella, OpenAI (OPAI.PVT) president Greg Brockman, Palantir (PLTR) CEO Alex Karp, Amazon (AMZN) founder Jeff Bezos, and others.

The gathering came as the US continues to digest a raft of alarming new AI disclosures in recent days, such as an Axios report that OpenAI, Anthropic, and security researchers were sifting through thousands of incidents of problematic actions by AI agents.

fullText:
President Donald Trump launched America.gov on Tuesday, unveiling what the administration has billed as a new AI-powered gateway to federal information and services that aims to streamline Americans' interactions with the government.

The website, which Trump introduced at Andrew W. Mellon Auditorium in Washington, features a chatbot-style interface that allows users to ask questions about government programs, benefits and services. The administration described America.gov as a "front door" to federal resources, consolidating information that is currently spread across dozens of agency websites.

"It's not just simply a website. It's a restoration of America's founding promise, and it's a reinvention of your government for the 21st century and beyond," Trump said at the rollout.

The debut of America.gov comes as policymakers, technology companies and privacy advocates continue to debate the expanding role of artificial intelligence in public-facing services. While AI tools have been touted for their ability to simplify complex tasks and improve access to information, experts have raised concerns about accuracy, transparency and data privacy, particularly when such systems are used to help people access government programs or services.

Asked at the announcement about risks associated with AI and centralized government services, Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services Administrator Mehmet Oz told Newsweek the administration does not want all user data stored in a single location. Instead, he described America.gov as a "federated system" in which individuals maintain control of their own records and choose whether to share them. Oz acknowledged that any system allowing access to sensitive information carries risks, but said federal officials are prioritizing cybersecurity and data protection as the platform evolves.

"We don't want all the information in one link," Oz said. "The real risk we have is if all your data is in one spot ... anyone who hacks it gets it all."

The president said Tuesday, "It cannot in theory be hacked into. And when they figure a way to do that, we'll end it, because they always figure a way, right?"

Joe Gebbia, U.S. chief design officer, said America.gov is powered by Google's Gemini and Elon Musk's Grok. Trump was joined by Musk, administration officials and tech leaders for the announcement.

Newsweek has reached out to the White House via email on Tuesday morning for comment.

Trump signed an executive order Tuesday that directs federal agencies to integrate their online services with America.gov, which the administration envisions as a single digital portal for accessing government information and completing transactions.

The White House said the platform will eventually allow users to perform tasks such as renewing passports and enrolling in Medicare, while Login.gov, the federal government's existing sign-in system, will be incorporated into the service.

The order applies to public-facing federal services used by more than 100,000 people annually, although IRS tax-filing services and certain national security-related functions are excluded.

"This is the American government working for the American people. Come to America.gov, tell us what you need. We'll help you get there and, ultimately, we'll help you get it done," Edward Frost, Administrator of the U.S. General Services Administration (GSA), told Newsweek at Tuesday's announcement.

The launch of America.gov also highlights the growing influence of Gebbia, the Airbnb co-founder whom Trump tapped in 2025 to lead the newly created National Design Studio. Established under the administration's "America by Design" initiative, the office is responsible for modernizing federal websites and digital services.

The chatbot-based America.gov portal represents one of the most visible examples of Gebbia's effort to apply Silicon Valley-style design principles to the federal government.

The launch of America.gov coincides with a high-profile White House gathering of some of the technology industry's most influential executives.

Trump will host a lunch focused on AI shortly after unveiling the new portal Attendees include Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, OpenAI co-founder Greg Brockman, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, Palo Alto Networks CEO Nikesh Arora and Altimeter Capital CEO Brad Gerstner.

The technology leaders joined Vice President JD Vance, House Speaker Mike Johnson, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles. The meeting comes as artificial intelligence is playing an increasingly prominent role in both the private and public sectors, with governments around the world grappling with how to harness the technology while addressing concerns about accuracy, privacy and security.

Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here.

Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Gabe Whisnant and Dave Siminoff.

fullText:
JERUSALEM - A slew of reports that Arab officials warned Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu about a serious threat emerging from Gaza days before the Oct. 7, 2023, attack by Hamas have put the longtime Israeli leader on the defensive less than 30 days before a pivotal election.

Ever since the attack, the most deadly in Israel's history, Netanyahu has argued that Israeli security chiefs collectively failed to foresee the surprise attack by Hamas - but that he led the fightback, scoring redemptive battlefield victories in Gaza, Lebanon, Syria and Iran.

But that narrative is fraying as reports of the advance warnings, including one delivered by United Arab Emirates President Mohamed bin Zayed al-Nahyan, train a spotlight on Netanyahu's handling of the attack and his refusal to allow an independent commission to investigate it.

Netanyahu and his office have denied the reports, and his political party and supporters have accused "left-wing" Israeli officials, as well as journalists and overseas interests, of conspiring to oust him from office through a coordinated smear campaign ahead of the Oct. 27 election.

The disclosures began to trickle out in early September, when the Israeli newspaper Haaretz published an excerpt from "Hostages: 843 Days of Abandonment," a book by two Israeli journalists that details an encrypted call reportedly made by the Emirati president, who is known as MBZ, less than two weeks before Oct. 7, 2023, to warn Netanyahu that Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar was planning a major operation that could destabilize the Middle East. Netanyahu did not pass on the warnings to his security aides, according to the book authors, Shlomi Eldar and Ruth Yuval.

"We have excellent proof and many more scoops in the book," Eldar said. "It's rock solid." The UAE Foreign Ministry did not deny the Haaretz excerpt, saying, "When necessary, all relevant intelligence has been and continues to be communicated between the relevant entities."

In recent days, the debate in Israel has reached a fever pitch after the Atlantic and the Wall Street Journal published reports that then-Egyptian intelligence chief Abbas Kamel also warned Netanyahu about Gaza in the days before Oct. 7.

On Sunday, Netanyahu flew to Abu Dhabi and requested that MBZ explicitly deny that a warning call about Oct. 7 took place in late 2023, said a person with knowledge of the meeting who, like others quoted in this article, spoke on the condition of anonymity due to the sensitivity of the matter.

Netanyahu's office denied that Netanyahu made such a request, calling it "fake news." When asked about the Sunday meeting, the UAE Foreign Ministry referred The Washington Post to a report by the official Emirates News Agency released late Monday saying the two leaders had discussed "bilateral relations and ways to strengthen ties." The ministry declined further comment.

Several senior Israeli officials, including the former army chief of staff and head of military intelligence, have resigned, saying they failed to protect the country.

Netanyahu, by contrast, has deflected responsibility and repeatedly accused his security chiefs of missing the threat from Gaza and even "deliberately" letting him sleep for four hours after Hamas began its assault on southern Israel at 6:30 a.m. on Oct. 7.

On Monday, Ronen Bar, the former director of Shin Bet, Israel's domestic intelligence agency, sued Netanyahu for defamation, accusing the prime minister of "trying to deflect fire from himself by hurling accusations at the person who warned him in real time."

It's not immediately clear how the allegations will affect polls, which have held relatively steady in recent weeks and show former military chief Gadi Eisenkot's party narrowly leading Netanyahu's Likud. The reports, however, have dominated headlines and prime-time talk shows.

Several security branches, including the Israel Defense Forces and Shin Bet, have conducted internal probes into their failures to anticipate the Oct. 7 attack, but Netanyahu's government has refused to authorize one for itself.

Many of Netanyahu's campaign rivals, including Eisenkot, have pledged to immediately establish an independent commission of inquiry if elected.

Jonathan Rynhold, a political scientist at Bar-Ilan University, said Netanyahu may be hobbled by the claims about the warnings, but his loyal base and Israel's predominantly right-leaning voters may not jump ship for the centrist bloc led by Eisenkot without a "clear smoking gun."

"Oct. 7 has been on everybody's mind every day for three years, so it is relevant, but these claims have been bubbling for a long time in different forms," Rynhold said. "Imagine there's a video of all the Egyptians and the Emiratis and you can actually see him getting the warning and it was repeated 50 times on social media, then it becomes unavoidable. But obviously that's not what's going to happen."

Sufian Abu Zaida, a former Palestinian official who was the source of the warning that eventually reached the UAE, told The Post that he met Sinwar, the Hamas leader, in his Gaza City office in September 2023, and Sinwar dictated an offer to Israeli negotiators: he would release two Israeli soldiers and two civilians held in Gaza in exchange for Israel freeing Palestinian prisoners and lifting its heavy trade and movement restrictions imposed on the strip since 2007. Otherwise, Sinwar warned, there would be an "earthquake."

"The exact content of the message was: "We will put cards on the table, there will be an earthquake regarding the negotiations and we will empty the [Israeli] prisons [of Palestinians]," Abu Zaida recalled in an interview this week, adding that Sinwar told him to "make sure" the message reached the Israelis.

Abu Zaida said he passed the message to Shin Bet officials and also relayed it to an adviser to MBZ in Abu Dhabi - the Palestinian politician Mohammad Dahlan, who then informed the UAE president. Abu Zaida said he also passed the message to Samir al-Mashharawi, a Palestinian political leader and Dahlan associate based in Egypt.

The three Palestinian intermediaries "didn't know that Sinwar was ready to go ahead with his threats, or how and when," Abu Zaida said. "I was thinking that it might be about the West Bank: kidnapping a soldier from here or there for later negotiations with Israel for a prisoner exchange."

Several months after Oct. 7, in early 2024, MBZ recounted to then-CIA Director William J. Burns that he had warned Netanyahu about the possibility of violence erupting but did not include specific details that anticipated the Oct. 7 plot, a person familiar with the matter said.

The Emirates' refusal to disavow the reports of advance warnings is particularly striking because it is the Arab country that has stood closest to Netanyahu over the past three years even as his international standing plummeted.

Since signing the Abraham Accords that normalized diplomatic relations with Israel in 2020, the UAE has often been more measured in its criticism of Israel's conduct in Gaza and the West Bank than some other Arab countries that have accused Israel of genocide and ethnic cleansing.

At other times, the UAE has taken a relatively tougher stance toward Israel's foes, such as Iran, and it has supported the U.S.-Israeli-led war.

Alex Vatanka, a senior fellow at the Middle East Institute in Washington, noted that Emirati officials have declined to hand Netanyahu a political favor by explicitly denying the reports of the warnings.

"The reality is that Netanyahu is a liability for the UAE right now," Vatanka said. "They are sensitive to their image in the Islamic world and don't want to be seen as too close with Netanyahu."

But, he added, the UAE is "not going to walk away from its relationship" with the state of Israel itself.

Back home, Netanyahu's supporters kicked into damage-control mode.

"As the elections approach, we are seeing a flood of false reports by mobilized left-wing journalists, aimed at toppling the right and installing a Left-Muslim Brotherhood government that will surrender on every front," the Likud Party said in a statement.

Amit Segal, a political commentator who is seen as close to Netanyahu, said there were "Arab nations" behind the "slanderous fabrications" and warned that if the Israeli right lost the elections, a Palestinian state would emerge.

"This is the election question: It is either the Right or Palestine," Segal posted on social media.

Eldar, the Israeli author, said Likud lawyers have threatened to sue him for defamation and accused him of seeking to influence the election. He said he first obtained information about the call almost two years ago and it took the publisher until this month to release the book.

"I would have preferred to publish it a year ago, but it took time," Eldar said.

One Israeli political consultant, who is not affiliated with a campaign in this election cycle and who spoke on the condition of anonymity to preserve client relationships, said Netanyahu's campaign might find ways to benefit from the fallout of the new claims.

The controversy could draw attention away from the intense criticism Netanyahu has faced over his government's policy of allowing ultra-Orthodox Jews to forgo mandatory military service, and Netanyahu could instead focus attention on Oct. 7 and the danger posed by Palestinian citizens of Israel, who make up about 21 percent of the Israeli population, the consultant said.

Polls show that to form a majority government, Eisenkot may need to join hands with the so-called Arab parties, which Netanyahu's campaign has frequently portrayed as security risks in campaign ads with racist undertones.

The furor over the pre-Oct. 7 warnings "seems negative, but it's also changed the narrative" in Israel, the consultant said. "Netanyahu can push aside the ultra-Orthodox issue and bring to the table the conversation about the fact that Gadi Eisenkot doesn't have a majority without the voice or fingers of the Arab parties."

Lior Soroka contributed to this report.

title: President Trump announces new $15 billion steel plant to be built in Iowa
description:
Washington — President Trump on Monday announced that the company Mesabi Metallics will build a $15 billion steel plant in Iowa over the coming years, in what would be the largest of its kind in U.S. history. 
"There's a company known as Mesabi," the president said in the Oval Office. "And they're going to make a big investment in a place called Iowa.
fullText:
Washington — President Trump on Monday announced that the company Mesabi Metallics will build a $15 billion steel plant in Iowa over the coming years, in what would be the largest of its kind in U.S. history.

"There's a company known as Mesabi," the president said in the Oval Office. "And they're going to make a big investment in a place called Iowa. I love Iowa. I won Iowa every time. Today, we're thrilled to announce that Mesabi Metallics will be building the largest steel plant in American history in the great state of Iowa."

The president and the Minnesota-based Mesabi Metallics unveiled the company's plans for what the White House is calling a mega steel plant, alongside Mesabi executives and Iowa officials. The announcement comes as several Iowa Republicans face competitive elections in the November midterms, including the party's candidates for Senate and governor.

Although Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick said Monday the steel plant won't receive direct federal support, he acknowledged that the government-run Export-Import Bank financed Mesabi's iron ore plant in Minnesota, which will provide the raw materials essential to making steel.

Once it's up and running in 2030, the plant is expected to produce 7.5 million or more tons of steel per year. A White House official said the plant is expected to create 1,750 permanent jobs in Iowa.

The plans for a new plant mark the Trump administration's latest move to boost domestic steel manufacturing in the face of overseas competition, a centerpiece of the president's trade agenda. Last year, he doubled tariffs on imported steel to 50%, and steel levies have been part of the ongoing trade dispute between the U.S. and Canada. He also approved a deal for Japan-based Nippon Steel to buy U.S. Steel, an arrangement that calls for new investments in the iconic Pittsburgh-based company.

Mesabi has not announced where in Iowa the steel plant will be, but Energy Secretary Chris Wright mentioned that it would be in the southeast part of the state. A White House official said this will be the first mega steel plant built in the U.S. since the 1960s. The Trump administration expects the steel could support U.S. defense projects in the future. The Wall Street Journal was first to report the president's anticipated announcement of the new steel plant.

The Export-Import Bank's board approved a $770 million direct loan to Mesabi Metallics for its iron ore endeavors on Sept. 24, a spokesperson for EXIM told CBS News. The board was initially considering up to $10 billion in support, according to a March news release.

Mesabi Metallics is owned by India-based Essar Group, but its operations haven't always been known as Mesabi Metallics.

In 2008, the Essar Group's Essar Steel Minnesota LLC began work on a massive iron mine and processing facility in Minnesota. But after years of delays, missed deadlines and financial challenges, Essar Steel Minnesota LLC filed for bankruptcy in 2016. Frustrated with the delays, the Minnesota Department of Natural Resources took steps in 2019 to potentially bar Essar Global from working with the state, although the company sued over that move, and the state ultimately did not complete the debarment process.

"This is a step in the right direction after northern Minnesotans have waited patiently — too patiently, in fact — for economic gains that have been dangled in front of their eyes for many years," Democratic state Reps. Julie Sandstede and Rob Ecklund said in a statement at the time.

What was known as Essar Steel Minnesota LLC was eventually reborn from the ashes of bankruptcy and was bought by Chippewa Capital Partners. But Essar Group eventually regained control starting in 2019.

CBS News has reached out to Mesabi Metallics and the Essar Group for comment.

State aid could potentially be on the way for Mesabi Metallics, too.

The Des Moines Register reported state lawmakers are being alerted they may need to return to the statehouse to approve tax breaks for Mesabi. CBS News has reached out to top members of the Iowa statehouse for comment.

"I'm so excited about this project," Iowa Sen. Joni Ernst said, thanking Mr. Trump and Essar.

It's not clear why the steel plant is in Iowa, instead of Minnesota, closer to the iron ore mine.

Iowa Republicans are facing competitive races for the U.S. House, Senate and governor's mansion. Republicans, who currently hold the governor's mansion and both Senate seats, are trying to fend off Democrats from changing that.

In the governor's race, Democratic Iowa State Auditor Rob Sand is facing off against Republican businessman Zach Lahn in what's expected to be a close race. In the open U.S. Senate seat being vacated by Sen. Joni Ernst's departure, Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson faces Democratic state lawmaker Josh Turek.

In the House, there are closely watched races in two Iowa congressional districts, between Republican Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks and Democratic former state Rep. Christina Bohannan, and between Republican Rep. Zach Nunn and Democratic state Sen. Sarah Trone Garriott.

Mr. Trump gave Hinson a shoutout in the Oval Office Monday, saying she will be "hopefully elected to the Senate, and she's outstanding." The president said he'll visit Iowa for a "great rally" there before the midterms.

A reporter asked the president why Republicans are having to work so hard to win seats in Iowa, a state he won by 13 points. The president said he thinks the polls, which show close statewide races in the Hawkeye State, are inaccurate.

"I don't know, I love Iowa," he said. "I've always been very strong with Iowa."

Andrew Bailey, the former Missouri attorney general who has supported debunked claims that the 2020 election was stolen, told bureau employees in an email that he was leaving to spend more time with this family, according to three people familiar with the personnel move who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss a matter they were not authorized to speak about.

Bailey, who was hired for the leadership role about a year ago, confirmed his departure in a social media post.

"With great pride in what we have accomplished, I am announcing that I am stepping down to return to my family in Missouri," Bailey wrote on social media. "I am confident Director Patel will continue to reform the FBI, combat violent crime, defend the homeland, ensure strong organizational accountability, and restore public trust in this institution of excellence."

The departure marks a dramatic turn for Bailey, a loyalist of President Donald Trump who had been floated as a candidate early in the administration to run the FBI or Justice Department.

It is also the latest shake-up at the federal law enforcement agency under FBI Director Kash Patel. Bailey was hired to serve as the co-deputy director alongside Dan Bongino, a conservative podcast host and former Secret Service officer.

Neither Bongino nor Bailey had FBI experience, which made them highly unusual picks for a position that typically goes to a veteran of the bureau. The position does not require Senate confirmation and is tasked with running the day-to-day operations of the FBI.

Earlier this year, Bongino quit amid frustrations about the demands of the position, The Washington Post previously reported. He was replaced with Christopher Raia, a career FBI official.

During Bailey's tenure, the department has seen an unprecedented wave of dismissals and transfers of experienced FBI agents.

Last week, for example, the top two agents running the counterterrorism division in the Washington field office were transferred because of their work investigating threats against Katie Miller - a conservative podcaster who is the wife of top Trump aide Stephen Miller - according to three people familiar with the matter.

The officials were transferred because top officials felt work on the probe was moving too slowly, said the people, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss a personnel matter.

Bailey resigned from his position as Missouri attorney general last September to assume the role as FBI co-deputy director.

He is a military veteran who as Missouri's chief legal officer mounted high-profile legal fights aligned with Trump's agenda. He sued Starbucks over its diversity, equity and inclusion policies; fought transgender care policies; and waged legal battles against "sanctuary city" policies.

Among the most notable parts of Bailey's short FBI tenure was his presence on the scene as the FBI executed search warrants in January to seize 2020 ballots and other election material from Fulton County, Georgia.

It is rare for an FBI deputy director to personally oversee such a routine development in an investigation, but Bailey's presence was also notable given the political tensions surrounding the probe and Trump's repeated insistence, without evidence, that the 2020 election was stolen. The FBI has said it is investigating whether what it has described in court filings as "deficiencies" in the 2020 vote tabulation in Fulton County, home to Atlanta, were the result of intentional wrongdoing that could constitute a crime.

title: Trump asked China's Xi if he wants to buy U.S. arms, ambassador says
description: — President Donald Trump has justified the pending U.S. arms sale to Taiwan to Chinese President Xi Jinping by downplaying it as just one of many sales Washington makes around the world — even asking Xi if he’d be in the market for U.S. arms, Trump’s ambassador to China said on Sunday.
fullText:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump has justified the pending U.S. arms sale to Taiwan to Chinese President Xi Jinping by downplaying it as just one of many sales Washington makes around the world — even asking Xi if he'd be in the market for U.S. arms, Trump's ambassador to China said on Sunday.

David Perdue said Trump raised the prospect of the arms sales from the U.S. to its ascendant geopolitical rival, an unlikely offer that if consummated would upend generations of U.S. policy toward China and Taiwan and potentially expose U.S. technology to a potential foe. Perdue, speaking to Shannon Bream on "Fox News Sunday" days after Trump hosted Xi for a state visit in Washington, didn't specify when the offer was made.

Bream had cited concerns from Republican and Democratic lawmakers over delayed aid packages and weapons orders to Taiwan, the self-ruled democracy, to defend itself from China's threat to invade the island. Bream asked if the U.S. is denying arms to Taiwan to appease the Chinese president, who visited Trump last week.

Perdue pushed back on the suggestion, stating that Trump "is as strong on Taiwan as I've ever seen anybody" and has sold it plenty of weapons. Perdue also said Trump and Xi continue to talk about future U.S. weapons sales to Taiwan.

"But President Trump continues to say, 'Hey, we sell arms to other people around the world,'" Perdue said. "He actually asked President Xi, would he like to buy some, at one point."

The U.S. is bound by its own laws to provide Taiwan with the means to defend itself. While not recognizing Taiwan as a country, the U.S. is the island's strongest informal backer and arms provider. But multiple U.S. leaders have left ambiguous whether they would commit military force to defend the U.S. ally should China invade.

China has pressed Washington to halt the arms sales, most prominently during a previous summit in May between Trump and Xi in Beijing. After that meeting, the United States paused the sale of a record-breaking $14 billion package — and Trump described arms sales to Taiwan as a "very good negotiating chip" with China.

In their private talks at the White House last week, Xi pressed Trump to oppose Taiwan independence, according to Chinese state media.

In Beijing, China's foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun did not confirm Perdue's remarks when asked about the matter on Monday. But he told reporters that China has always strengthened its national defense capabilities based on its needs, and is committed to maintaining world peace and stability.

title: 32 things we learned in NFL Week 3: Bills don't look good, literally or figuratively
description: Every season, the team's winless and undefeated teams draw a lot of scrutiny after two weeks – uet that script tends to flip, as it did Sunday in Washington.
fullText:
The 32 things we learned from Week 3 of the 2026 NFL season:

0(-3). That would be a reference to the league's winless teams, of which there are five (Houston Texans, Miami Dolphins, Los Angeles Chargers, Tampa Bay Buccaneers and Tennessee Titans) now saddled with that weighty record − one only seven teams in league history have overcome to make the playoffs. The Texans managed to do it in 2025, but no club has ever pulled it off in successive seasons. (But worth noting that Houston is the only team in the 21st century to surmount the 0-3 challenge, also pulling it off in 2018.)

1. Back to that familiar question that's pervaded the early part of the 2026 season: Who's No. 1? It's now a tough case to make for the reigning champion Seattle Seahawks after they lost at Washington to a team without its starting quarterback. The Buffalo Bills were fortunate to survive the winless Chargers, QB Josh Allen playing a terrible game in a terrible uniform … more on those fronts later. The undefeated San Francisco 49ers? Can they field a functional team next week? Ready to make a case for the Las Vegas Raiders or Minnesota Vikings, who are also 3-0? Ready to re-anoint the dynastic Kansas City Chiefs ... despite a fairly ugly win at feckless Miami? Check nfl.usatoday.com on Tuesday morning once the dust has fully settled … and our next batch of power rankings are out of the oven.

1a. Prior to Sunday's game against the Baltimore Ravens in Rio de Janeiro, the Dallas Cowboys had appeared in one international game – the fewest in NFL history. But they may have also participated in the best international game in league history. Keep reading ...

(QB)2: Kudos to backups Marcus Mariota and Jameis Winston, who led the Commanders and New York Giants, respectively, to wins Sunday – a week after both teams lost their starting quarterbacks, the Giants' Jaxson Dart expected to miss the rest of the season. Next up? Chicago Bears veteran backup Case Keenum, who is expected to start Monday night against the Philadelphia Eagles in place of injured Caleb Williams.

3(-0). Five teams currently sport that spotless record (49ers, Bills, Chiefs, Raiders and Vikings). Philly can join their ranks Monday night with a win at Soldier Field.

4. The number of consecutive seasons an 0-2 team knocked off a 2-0 team, which happened Sunday when the Commanders ambushed the Seahawks, who won 38-14 at Northwest Stadium last November. And the upset came amid Seattle QB Sam Darnold's return from his Week 1 gluteal injury − and he played his butt off Sunday with 379 yards and four TDs through the air.

5. The number of turnovers committed by the Bills on Sunday, three courtesy of Allen. It was Buffalo's first win with that many giveaways since 1997. Good thing Buffalo's defense finally showed up, even if the Bolts offense didn't ... again.

5a. Ugly a game as he had, Allen became the first QB in NFL history with multiple rushing TDs in three consecutive games.

6. The number of TD receptions by Seahawks WR Jaxon Smith-Njigba, who's excelling, per usual, no matter which of his quarterbacks is throwing to him. The 2025 Offensive Player of the Year is on a very early pace to shatter Hall of Famer Randy Moss' single-season record (23 TD grabs in 2007).

Jaxon Smith-Njigba has had 120+ receiving yards and 1+ receiving TD in each of his team's first 3 games 🫨

The only other player to accomplish that in NFL history is HOF Jerry Rice@Seahawks | #GoHawks pic.twitter.com/nVNt719IkI

7. However it appears the Detroit Lions' Jahmyr Gibbs is going to give JSN a run for his money when it comes to capturing 2026 OPOY honors. Gibbs, who posted 164 yards and three touchdowns from scrimmage in Sunday's 31-24 defeat of the New York Jets, is off to a historic start.

.@Lions RB Jahmyr Gibbs is the first player in @NFL history to produce the following statistics through the first 3 games of any season:

- 300 rushing yards
- 4 rushing TDs
- 150 receiving yards
- 2 receiving TDs#OnePride pic.twitter.com/YGj3AZSIMe

8. The jersey number of four-time NFL MVP Aaron Rodgers, who passed for at least 290 yards (292) and multiple TDs (3) for the first time as a Pittsburgh Steeler in Sunday's 30-27 escape from the Cincinnati Bengals, who still haven't started 3-0 since 2015.

9. Number of consecutive games lost by the Indianapolis Colts, the longest skid in the league going back to last season … prior to Sunday's narrow victory over Houston.

10. Weird zero stat of the day: Cleveland Browns backup QB Shedeur Sanders completed his only pass of the day for 0 yards. That translates to a passer rating of 79.2, which is significantly better than Carolina Panthers counterpart Bryce Young's on Sunday (70.7, even though Young completed 26 of 48 passes for 291 yards, a TD and an INT). Sanders' 79.2 would have even led the league back in the old, pre-Super Bowl era (before 1966) days.

11. Weirdest zero stat of the day: Niners WR Deebo Samuel had 80 receiving yards and a TD in Sunday's win … despite finishing with zero receptions. Explanation? He scored the game's first touchdown on a hook-and-lateral with WR Mike Evans, who was credited with a 2-yard catch on the play.

HOOK-AND-LADDER TD 🤯

Deebo Samuel traveled a total distance of 110.35 yards and reached a max speed of 20.39 MPH on this 80-yard touchdown, per @NextGenStats @AZvsSF on FOX/FOX One
Stream on #NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/88dsZtSZum

11a. Samuel also iced San Francisco's 36-30 victory over the Arizona Cardinals with another uncredited catch.

Deebo ices it on the hands team 👏@AZvsSF on FOX/FOX One
Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/t32MJ70YM6

12. Number of consecutive games won by the Seahawks, the longest heater in the league going back to last season … prior to Sunday's loss to the Commanders. Seattle failed to become the third consecutive Super Bowl champion to begin its title defense with a 3-0 start.

13. Alternate uniforms < throwback uniforms.

It's merely a rule of thumb, not an immutable law. But if you saw the Bills ("Nickel City") and Colts ("Anvil Strike") unis on Sunday, then you'd probably agree that gray is a good color for baseball roadies … not so much for NFL uniforms.

The @BuffaloBills' "Nickel City" uniforms are ready for their debut. @LACvsBUF on FOX/FOX One
Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/SWjFLvF6Jw

14. However the Jacksonville Jaguars' throwbacks? Sweet. Can we get those back as the primaries?

The Jaguars "Prowler" throwbacks should be their primary uniforms. I will die on this hill without regrets. pic.twitter.com/7b7Sj2Kyhq

15. Speaking of bad looks, what's the tougher watch on TV: Indy's Lucas Oil Stadium with the roof open on a sunny day – like Sunday – or AT&T Stadium with the sun streaming through its western end-zone windows?

16. The Cowboys didn't have to deal with any glare – or even a bad field – Sunday while facing the Ravens at Maracanã Stadium in the league's first foray into Rio. But their problematic defense sabotaged them yet again – surrendering a 27-yard completion to Zay Flowers on the game's final game from scrimmage … before Ravens K Tyler Loop drilled the game-winning 56-yarder to secure a 34-31 victory. Still, this was a fantastic game and, who's to say, perhaps a Super Bowl 61 preview based on how this unpredictable season has unfolded so far.

17. Congratulations to Jaguars CB/WR Travis Hunter, who notched his first career interception Sunday … albeit on a – another – terrible throw by New England Patriots QB Drake Maye. Ten games into his career, Hunter, the insanely hyped dual-threat, Heisman Trophy-winning star from the University of Colorado, has one career pick and one career TD. I've been as skeptical as anyone about his pro prognosis, but good to see a player – and a great young man by many accounts – have a highlight moment.

TRAVIS HUNTER FIRST CAREER INT ‼️@NEvsJAX on CBS/Paramount+
Stream on #NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/tZFgPtUIf4

18. Did you know Jacksonville has a Brian Thomas Jr. and Bryan Thomas Jr. on its roster? Brian, the better-known wideout, had one catch for 8 yards in the Jags' 35-6 rout of the Patriots. Bryan, a defensive end, was credited with a tackle and half-sack of Maye.

19. Jaguars K Cam Little, who hit a 70-yard field goal in preseason last year and also broke the official record with a 68-yarder in the regular season last November, nearly hit a 70-yarder that counted right before halftime Sunday … but was wide right by inches. It's coming, though.

Cam Little attempts a record-breaking 70-yard field goal but it is no good.#NFL pic.twitter.com/obwBsaikJF

Cam Little thought his 70-yarder was good against the Patriots:

“Out of the 67, the 68, and the 70 that I’ve attempted, I by far hit that ball the cleanest by a mile.”#Jaguars #DUUUVAL @BrentASJax pic.twitter.com/3t6bA9wCZm

20. "Browns are gonna Browns?" Admittedly, I poked fun at first-year Cleveland coach Todd Monken for getting worked up about NBC analyst Mike Tomlin's dig prior to the Browns' win at Tampa last week. But maybe it's a positive phrase? Whatever you think of QB Deshaun Watson on a human level, he's got his team off to a 2-1 start after engineering Sunday's fourth-quarter win over the Panthers.

21. "Kinda poetic that I get this highlight," Tomlin said, the longtime Steelers coach, said on "Football Night in America," while breaking down the Browns' second consecutive win.

22. Watson, who's been a reviled figure in Cleveland essentially since his disastrous 2022 acquisition, was actually cheered Sunday, including when he returned after missing a play on a roughing penalty that preceded his game-winning TD pass to TE Harold Fannin Jr.

23. "I got a little teary-eyed feeling that energy because I put so much work to get back here, to be in this moment, to show that I can finish these games and get W's for the city and this organization," Watson said following the win.

24. The undefeated Raiders have already matched last season's win total (3), which is what allowed them to draft QB Fernando Mendoza atop the 2026 draft.

25. Not that Las Vegas has needed the 2025 Heisman Trophy winner as veteran Kirk Cousins has tossed three TDs in all three of the Silver and Black's victories, including Sunday's come-from-behind effort in New Orleans.

26. That's because the Saints had been dominant in the fourth quarter, outscoring opponents 25-3 in the final period over the first two weeks. But the Raiders outpointed them 13-0 in the fourth in Sunday's 35-27 win at the Superdome.

27. And while second-year Saints QB Tyler Shough threw four TD passes Sunday, he also turned the ball over three times, giving Cousins and the Raiders the margin for error they needed to snatch the victory.

28. Call the Raiders' start fluky if you want, but remember that Sunday was the first game this season in which they had, arguably, their best player – TE Brock Bowers making his 2026 debut to the tune of 10 catches, 116 yards and a TD. He missed the first two weeks after undergoing a meniscus trim.

29. Call the Vikings' 3-0 start fluky if you want – especially in light of injuries to QB Kyler Murray, WR Justin Jefferson (Sunday) and others. They also needed a punt return for a TD in their 23-16 win at Tampa on Sunday. But that Minnesota D is vicious – racking up six sacks and 12 QB hits Sunday while knocking Bucs QB Baker Mayfield from the game.

30. If you didn't know, Mayfield's backup is undrafted rookie Jalon Daniels, who threw a pick among three incompletions in his pro debut. The Bucs' ship sure appears to be sinking fast while going to the bottom of the NFC South standings, especially after Mayfield suffered a dislocated thumb on his throwing hand.

31. A reminder to all NFL players, officials and writers: "You guys better get your (expletive) together" … which is what referee Ronald Torbert told his crew (on a hot mic) during Sunday's game in Indianapolis, per the Associated Press.

32. Last and, sadly, least – the Dolphins. Not only are the Fins winless, they haven't come closer than 14 points to a victory. Perhaps worse, RB De'Von Achane, their best player, suffered a knee injury that seems to be serious, coach Jeff Hafley admitting a lack of optimism about Achane's prognosis. Could we be witnessing the first 0-17 outfit in NFL history?

title: Three Takeaways from Washington Football's 27-24 Loss to Minnesota
description: Washington's ugly 27-24 loss to Minnesota taught the Big Ten a lot about Jedd Fisch's Huskies.
fullText:
The Washington Huskies' Big Ten opener wasn't kind to them, as they fell to the Minnesota Golden Gophers 27-24 on Saturday night. Although the scoreboard indicates a tightly contested affair between the two teams, the play on the field showed something else.

Here are three takeaways following a disappointing performance from Jedd Fisch's team.

Entering the season, Washington's offensive line was very vocal about its aspirations for the season, including competing for the Joe Moore Award, which is given to the nation's best offensive line. Through four games, the group hasn't come anywhere close to being in that conversation, with its worst performance of the season coming on Saturday night.

The Golden Gophers recorded 7 sacks on the evening to go along with 9 tackles for loss and just 40 rushing yards allowed. The Huskies were once again unable to find any sort of success on the ground, forcing quarterback Demond Williams Jr. and the offense into obvious passing situations. Even then, the second-year starter seemed uncomfortable in the pocket for a majority of the game, in part due to the pressure he faced from a resilient Minnesota front seven.

While the Huskies' next opponent, USC, offers a "bend but don't break" defense, the offensive line hasn't shown much to be optimistic about thus far.

After giving up two touchdowns in the opening period, Ryan Walters' defense was able to hold the Golden Gophers to just 13 points for the rest of the game. The X-factor, however, was Minnesota's ability to control the clock and gain timely yardage proved pivotal throughout the second half. Junior TJ Thomas led the Gophers' rushing attack with 78 yards and averaged 7.1 yards per carry, while the team ran for 125 yards.

While the numbers don't seem staggering, Thomas broke tackles all night and put the Husky defense on its heels, as UW logged at least 11 missed tackles. Coach P.J. Fleck was able to establish his brand of football early and often after jumping out to an early 14-0 lead, winning the time-of-possession battle by over 12 minutes. In order to turn things around entering back-to-back games against ranked opponents, the Washington front seven will have to put a major emphasis on bringing ball carriers down at the first point of contact.

Another running back injury, Julian McMahan, who was spotted in a walking boot before the game, is out for the season

Injuries have plagued the Huskies throughout the early part of the season, primarily at the running back position. While the loss of Quaid Carr and Jayden Limar has certainly changed the dynamic of the offense, it was the Washington defense that showed vulnerability due to some key injuries. Starting corner Emmanuel Karnley and safety Rahshawn Clark were listed as "emergency options" entering the contest, and the Gophers' quarterback Drake Lindsey took advantage of it.

Third-year cornerback Elias Johnson was the main victim, giving up two passing touchdowns in the first quarter. While Karnley didn't see any action in the contest, Clark was the primary punt and kickoff returner, but did not play on defense. With quarterback Drake Lindsey throwing for over 200 yards and three scores, Walters' secondary surely could've used two of their key starters. While Karnley and Clark are both expected to return full-time soon, the Huskies need as many reinforcements as possible as they stare down a gauntlet of conference games.

Fisch and company will look to bounce back from the underwhelming performance, but it won't be easy, as Washington heads south to take on No. 18 USC next Saturday.

title: Lawrence throws 3 TD passes as Jaguars rout Patriots and raise more questions about Maye
description: Trevor Lawrence threw three touchdown passes, including one on which Parker Washington made a fingertip catch in the end zone, and the Jacksonville Jaguars bounced back from their worst offensive performance in nearly a year to dominate New England 35-6.
fullText:
Trevor Lawrence threw three touchdown passes, including one on which Parker Washington made a fingertip catch in the end zone, and the Jacksonville Jaguars bounced back from their worst offensive performance in nearly a year to dominate New England 35-6 on Sunday.

Lawrence also strangely gave himself up at the 1-yard line with nearly 9 minutes to play. It created countless laughs on the sideline. Bhayshul Tuten scored on the next play, which surely will cause angst in the fantasy football world.

Regardless, the Jaguars (2-1) won their sixth consecutive regular-season game at home and raised more questions about Drake Maye's regression for the Patriots.

Maye fumbled twice, losing one, and threw two more interceptions before getting pulled in the fourth quarter with the game out of reach. He now has one TD pass and six INTs in three games. He threw 31 touchdowns and eight picks last season for the AFC champion Patriots (1-2).

Maye's performance in this one was more alarming than his three-interception fourth quarter in the season opener at Seattle. The ball slipped out of his right hand with no one around him during one play. He threw into coverage on a third-and-goal play, resulting in Travis Hunter's first career interception. He also threw a pass directly to cornerback Jarrian Jones that set up another score for Jacksonville.

New England had other issues, too: Andy Borregales missed a 38-yard field goal; Kyle Williams mistakenly stepped out of bounds on a kickoff return, giving the Pats the ball at their 9-yard line; and Mack Hollins was flagged for taunting at the end of a 9-yard reception, turning a fourth-and-1 play into a field-goal situation.

The Jaguars were much cleaner all afternoon.

Lawrence completed 19 of 29 passes for 182 yards, with an interception on a tipped pass. He connected with Jakobi Meyers and Josh Cameron for TDs. Cameron got significant snaps in place of Brian Thomas Jr., who dropped two passes in last week's 20-13 loss at Denver.

Tuten finished with 73 yards rushing.

Facing a first-and-30 play after back-to-back penalties, the Patriots dialed up some trickiness in Jacksonville territory. And it worked despite a lot of adversity.

Maye threw a backward pass to Elton Chism III, who had to elude Jones' tackle near the sideline. Chism stayed on his feet and completed a pass to Mack Hollins that was tipped by cornerback Travis Hunter. It was far from pretty but resulted in a 16-yard gain that led to a field goal.

Jacksonville's Cam Little just missed making a 70-yard field goal, which would have broken his NFL record. Little attempted the long kick at the end of the first half and pushed it just a couple feet right.

Little had the distance, which was no surprise considering he made a 70-yard in a preseason game against Pittsburgh in 2025. He set the real NFL mark later that year with a 68-yarder at Las Vegas in early November.

Patriots: RG Greg Van Roten left in the first half with a thigh injury and did not return. DT Christian Barmore (shoulder) and CB Carlton Davis III also missed snaps but later returned.

Jaguars: DT DaVon Hamilton stayed on the ground in pain after sacking Maye but was able to return a few plays later.

Patriots: Play at Buffalo next Sunday.

Jaguars: Play at Cincinnati next Sunday.

title: Ex-CIA officer's novel alleges grave dysfunction in deep-cover operations
description:

Though often fantastical, it contains thinly veiled true-life details about the inner workings of the agency’s spying operations, according to former CIA officials.

fullText:
A new, previously suppressed book by a former CIA officer paints a satirical and slashing portrait of the agency's deep-cover spying program as riven by systematic dysfunction.

The book, "The Pickle Factory," written by an ex-CIA nonofficial cover officer, under the pen name Sam R. Oyken, is billed as a work of fiction. Though often fantastical, it contains thinly veiled true-life details about the inner workings of the agency's spying operations, according to former CIA officials.

Most CIA officers work under what's known as "official cover" and generally masquerade as U.S. diplomats abroad. NOCs, who often pose as businessmen or consultants, have no overt connections to the U.S. government and therefore operate without diplomatic immunity.

Because of the potential dangers of their missions and the clandestine participation of American companies who provide cover to these officers, NOCs' operations are closely guarded inside the CIA.

"The Pickle Factory," published in late July, is the culmination of what the author characterized as a multiyear battle against agency censors, who first rejected publication of the manuscript in 2014. The Washington Post is referring to him by his pen name, as the former NOC remains undercover.

Former CIA employees are required to submit all work potentially relevant to their agency careers to the CIA's Prepublication Classification Review Board for potential redaction, to expunge it of allegedly classified information.

"They insisted for years after I submitted the manuscript of my novel that I couldn't publish a single word, a straight-up First Amendment violation," said Oyken in an interview.

Then-CIA Executive Director Meroe Park reversed the blanket ban in 2017, but the agency then "tried to redact more than half of the book, which I fought, redaction by redaction, until they folded," he said.

Park did not return a request for comment. A spokesperson for the CIA declined to comment.

The saga surrounding the book first trickled into public view in 2015, when Oyken - then using the alias Mack Charles in court documents - lodged a $25 million complaint against the CIA in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, alleging that agency officials conspired to fire the 13-year CIA veteran because they disapproved of his romantic relationship with another deep-cover officer to whom he was engaged and who was two decades younger.

Oyken was fired from the CIA in December 2010 and accused the agency of suppressing his book as part of a broader retaliation campaign, according to the 2015 lawsuit.

His suit against the agency was dismissed on procedural grounds in March 2016. The passage of time, and changes in agency leadership, appear to have attenuated concerns surrounding the book, and the CIA gave Oyken final approval to publish "The Pickle Factory" in early 2026.

Books by former NOCs have often met fierce resistance inside the CIA.

The 2019 publication of "Life Undercover," a memoir by former deep-cover officer Amaryllis Fox Kennedy, became embroiled in controversy when reports emerged that she did not receive final CIA approval to publish her book. Fox Kennedy - who served until recently as a senior official within the Office of the Director of National Intelligence and the Office of Management and Budget inside the Trump administration - did not appear to face sanction by the agency.

The CIA did sue another ex-NOC, writing under the pen name Ishmael Jones, for publishing a critical 2008 nonfiction account of his own experience inside the deep-cover program. Jones's book, "The Human Factor," had not been reviewed by agency censors. In 2012, a federal judge ordered Jones to forfeit any profit from future sales of the book.

"The Pickle Factory" dredges up what many CIA alumni consider an unhappy chapter in the history of the agency's deep-cover program.

In addition to skewering a number of former senior agency officials who oversaw the NOC cadre - whose biographies (and, at times, names) are only lightly fictionalized - the book recounts the agency's post-9/11 push to procure, and perhaps surreptitiously redirect for other purposes, billions of dollars in funding earmarked by Congress for a vastly expanded NOC program.

The post-9/11 NOC expansion was a real-life "debacle," said a former deep-cover colleague of Oyken's, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to candidly address sensitive intelligence operations, "where results were secondary, receipts were primary, and spending was king."

Much of Oyken's work with the agency remains shrouded in secrecy. His career bridged two eras at CIA, according to the same former colleague: the bespoke, targeted deep-cover program extant at CIA before Sept. 11, 2001, and the engorged NOC program that followed it, with younger, poorly trained NOCs being rushed into the field.

One part of this initiative involved deploying groups of these new NOCs to roughly a dozen secret "platforms" abroad; by 2008, almost all these efforts had folded in failure.

Oyken joined the CIA in 1996 as a French-speaking graduate of Harvard Law School who worked for the white-shoe law firm Covington & Burling before joining the agency, according to a declassified tranche of documents reviewed by The Post.

In 1999, he was selected for a 20-year deep-cover assignment abroad, an unusually long posting for NOC officers. The documents, some of which were redacted, point to a posting somewhere in Europe.

That assignment was cut short for reasons unclear in the declassified tranche reviewed by The Post. The mission ended because of a counterintelligence issue unrelated to Oyken's performance, according to another former CIA official who spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe clandestine operations. Oyken was subsequently assigned to be an instructor to CIA trainees, according to the documents.

He was then selected for a managerial role inside the NOC program, according to court documents as well as the declassified tranche reviewed by The Post. Oyken is identified in the declassified papers as a "QRN," which former CIA colleagues say refers to "Quick Reaction NOC," an elite group of deep-cover officers who often travel on non-U.S. passports to undertake highly sensitive intelligence-gathering or eavesdropping-related missions abroad.

The court documents suggest that, after his stint as a trainer, Oyken served as QRN chief, stating that he "exercised supervisory authority over more than 80 subordinates, including other NOC Operations Officers in his Group."

Oyken's dismissal from the CIA was a contentious and bitter affair, per both sets of documents. His overseers accused him of financial improprieties, inappropriate romantic relationships with subordinates, absenteeism in his managerial duties and bullying of underlings. Agency officials also lamented his lack of recruitments, according to the declassified tranche.

His was "a chronic case of long-term behavior that has completely eroded the confidence management has in this officer," said one declassified agency memorandum reviewed by The Post.

Oyken strenuously contested the allegations. "They came at me like a pack of wild dogs," he said in an interview.

The declassified documents reveal an aggressive investigation into Oyken, including his finances. In one partially redacted 2009 email, an incoming NOC program chief decries the "loose approach" to deep-cover deployments, vowing that Oyken "will be coming home the first day I'm in the chair." He was "the kind of china I'm looking forward to breaking" upon taking over the program, writes the soon-to-be NOC boss.

Oyken characterizes the deep-cover program as hidebound and in acute need of reform. "There's a certain kind of CIA manager who prefers that NOCs be full-time accountants rather than spies out taking risks," he said. "Meanwhile they themselves squander billions of dollars and turn a blind eye while their cronies make off with stacks of gold bars."

In May 2026, David J. Rush, a senior CIA official working on ultrasecret intelligence-gathering programs, was arrested on charges of stealing public funds, including the alleged theft of $40 million worth of gold bars from the agency.

Though formally a work of fiction, "The Pickle Factory" clearly puts the real-world CIA in its crosshairs. "It's almost impossible for outsiders to grasp how mediocre the agency has become," Oyken said. "Only a novel-length treatment could do the topic justice."

fullText:
TAIPEI, Sept 27 (Reuters) - The United States "very much" understands Taiwan's defence needs and the severe military threat it faces from China, a senior ‌Taiwanese diplomat said on Sunday, following a Washington summit between the US ‌and Chinese leaders.

Democratically governed Taiwan, which China claims as its own territory, has been waiting for months ​for US President Donald Trump to approve a new arms sales package worth some $14 billion, following up on a record $11 billion deal unveiled last December.

After meeting Chinese President Xi Jinping in Beijing in May, Trump said he was keeping the latest arms ‌sales package in abeyance. Trump ⁠has not mentioned the sale since last week's summit, saying only on Saturday that Xi understands his position on Taiwan.

Speaking to ⁠reporters in Taipei, Taiwan Deputy Foreign Minister Chen Ming-chi pointed to comments by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio that military sales to anyone require the same careful consideration.

"Taiwan ​faces a ​severe situation in the Taiwan Strait. Even ​though China's economy is declining, ‌it continues investing more resources into building military capacity. Under this context, the US very much understands our defence needs," he said.

Washington also understands Taiwan's determination to invest in its military, Chen added.

"We do continuously communicate with them, and we believe the US understands the situation we face and our determination on defence investment completely."

The ‌United States is bound by law to provide ​Taiwan with the means to defend itself. China ​has repeatedly called for military ​sales to end.

David Perdue, the US ambassador to China, told CNBC ‌on Friday that there has been ​no change in Taiwan ​policy by Trump, including on arms sales.

Chen said Taiwan had received confirmation "from our American friends repeatedly that US policy toward Taiwan remains unchanged".

Taiwan's government ​rejects Beijing's sovereignty claims, saying ‌only the island's people can decide their future.

China has rebuffed repeated calls ​for talks by Taiwan President Lai Ching-te, whom it calls a "separatist".

(Reporting ​by Ben Blanchard; Editing by Jamie Freed)

Two giant pandas sent by China arrived in the United States on Sunday, Beijing's state media said, after a leaders' summit that was heavy on symbolism and light on major breakthroughs.

The pandas' transfer had already been agreed but the departure was announced Thursday during Chinese President Xi Jinping's visit to Washington.

The black-and-white mammals are immensely popular around the world, and China loans them out as part of a "panda diplomacy" programme to foster foreign ties.

Ping Ping and Fu Shuang departed from Chengdu Shuangliu International Airport on a chartered flight at around 3:00 am (1900 GMT on Saturday), state news agency Xinhua reported.

After a 16-hour flight that crossed the international date line, the bears touched down in Atlanta, Georgia shortly before 7:00 am local time (1100 GMT on Sunday), Xinhua said later.

Steamed corn buns, bamboo shoots and carrots were prepared to keep the pandas nourished during their flight, Chinese state-run media the Global Times reported.

The Boeing 777 operated by FedEx was the top-tracked aircraft on aviation information platform FlightRadar24 as it neared Alaska, roughly halfway into its journey.

The pandas will be hosted by Zoo Atlanta for the next 10 years.

A farewell ceremony was held for the pair before their departure by the Chengdu Research Base of Giant Panda Breeding.

Experienced keepers were dispatched by the US side to accompany the duo on their flight, the Global Times reported.

In preparation for their arrival, Zoo Atlanta has renovated its panda facilities and assembled a team of animal caretakers.

It has also ensured a stable and long-term supply of bamboo, grown locally in Atlanta, which has a climate that is very similar to Chengdu.

Zoo Atlanta previously hosted pandas on loan from China for a quarter of a century starting in 1999, but it has not had any since 2024.

Both arrivals were born in 2020. Ping Ping, a male, is now six years old while Fu Shuang, a female, will turn six next month.

Pandas in captivity typically live for around 30 years.

Beijing has sent the furry creatures across the globe for decades as soft-power ambassadors of its diplomatic goodwill.

In 1972, China gifted a pair of pandas to Washington, following US president Richard Nixon's historic visit to the Communist nation.

Beijing recalled two of its pandas from Japan early this year, following a diplomatic spat that began when Japan's prime minister hinted that Tokyo could intervene militarily in the event of any attack on Taiwan.

fullText:
Two veteran FBI agents overseeing counterterrorism operations in the nation’s capital have been removed from their jobs and reassigned over the handling of an investigation involving Katie Miller, the conservative podcaster and wife of senior White House adviser Stephen Miller, according to two people familiar with the move.

Michael Burgwald, the special agent in charge of counterterrorism matters at the FBI’s Washington Field Office, and his deputy, Courtland Rae, were ousted from their positions by bureau leadership after investigators determined that allegedly harassing phone calls Katie Miller received from unknown individuals did not warrant further investigation, the sources said.

The field office team that reviewed the reported harassing calls determined they did not meet the threshold required for an FBI investigation, and no nexus to terrorism was identified, the sources said. This decision did not sit well with bureau leadership, and the two senior field office agents were removed from their positions, according to the sources.

Since taking office last year, FBI director Kash Patel — a fierce loyalist of President Donald Trump — has fired, demoted, or forced into retirement countless career employees who handled past investigations into Trump and his allies. Many of those forced out have filed lawsuits seeking reinstatement.

In a statement on an official FBI “Rapid Response” social media account established to tout the agency and respond to critics, Darren Cox, the senior executive who oversees the bureau’s DC office, confirmed the ousting of Burgwald and Rae, but denied the order came from Patel.

“This was a personnel decision made at the Washington field office level alone based on our constant evaluation of mission needs,” Cox said. “Any suggestion otherwise is false.”

CNN is attempting to locate contact information for Burgwald and Rae. The decision to remove them from their positions has riled many rank and file FBI employees who have been critical of personnel moves they view as highly politicized, sources said.

Burgwald graduated from the United States Military Academy West Point and was the recipient of FBI investigative awards, while Rae similarly rose through the ranks of the organization after a lengthy career in national security, sources said.

The reassignment of the two senior officials was first reported by Bloomberg Law.

CNN has reached out to the White House for comment. In a statement to Bloomberg Law, White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said Stephen and Katie Miller had no interaction with Burgwald or Rae, adding, “Senior leadership at the FBI determined they were stifling investigations into very serious threats and made a unilateral decision to remove them.”

Still, there is a history of the Millers expressing their displeasure at the FBI’s handling of personal incidents they viewed as threatening in nature. According to people familiar with an incident last year, the couple grew irate with FBI officials over pushback by career agents to use bureau resources to investigate paper flyers critical of Stephen Miller that were posted in the family’s neighborhood. Like several senior Trump officials, the couple later moved into military housing.

CNN’s Aleena Fayaz contributed to this report.

title: “In Great Spirits”: Dream HC Weighs In on Angel Reese After She Was Cleared to Play in the Playoff Opener
description: Getting hit in the face is not going to stop Angel Reese from playing in her first-ever playoff game. fullText:
Getting hit in the face is not going to stop Angel Reese from playing in her first-ever playoff game. As the Atlanta Dream get ready to face the Washington Mystics in the first round of the playoffs, coach Karl Smesko has hinted that they might have Reese back in action for the first game, as the Dream management has taken her off the injury report.

"She seems to be in great spirits. She's had a couple of really good practices. I think she's excited about being in the playoffs this time of year," Smesko said on Saturday, just a day before the Dream face the Mystics. "We all know how great she's been; she's been great all year, down the stretch, she's been."

There was some speculation around Reese's status after her abrupt exit in the win against the New York Liberty on Wednesday night. With just around 5.6 seconds left in the second quarter of the game, Reese took an elbow to the face from Liberty's Sabrina Ionescu.

The play was immediately reviewed by the officials, and the foul was upgraded to a flagrant one. While Reese came back from the locker room to make two of her free throws, she exited again and did not feature for the rest of the game, although she did return to the bench with around 6:19 left in the third quarter.

Angel Reese's got the Dream playing their best basketball right now. 

"She was cleared, but we made a decision that it would be smart for her to sit out the second half," HC Karl Smesko said after the game.

Having Reese back is certainly good news for this Atlanta team. They have qualified as the fourth seed with a 30-14 record, and Angel Reese has been a towering figure in their frontcourt.

Reese has made herself indispensable in Atlanta's tactical gameplay, averaging a career-high 16.4 points per game, but it's her contributions in the paint and around the rim that have earned her several WNBA milestones this season. Contributing 12.1 rebounds while adding 2.8 assists and 1.8 steals per game, she extended her league record for most double-doubles in a season, with her 32nd double-double on Monday against the Liberty.

This also moved her level with Hall of Famer Yolanda Griffith for 12th on the WNBA's all-time double-doubles list.

Earlier in the month, Reese became the first player in WNBA history to surpass 500 rebounds in a single season. She currently has 521 rebounds this season, and Reese has hinted that she has no intention of taking her foot off the accelerator.

"Anything that goes up is mine," she said on August 24. "I want to be one of (the best) when I walk away from the game. So just being able to … be consistent every night is something I'm looking forward to doing."

Coupling Reese's dominance in the paint with some efficient shooting from Rhyne Howard, the Dream has all the pieces to make a deep playoff run. With four different players—Allisha Gray, Rhyne Howard, Angel Reese, and Jordin Canada—scoring in double digits throughout the season, Atlanta has shown that they are not dependent on any one player for its output.

However, ruling out the Washington Mystics, who have been the surprise package in the WNBA this year, would be a mistake.

Riding on a young core of stars such as Sonia Citron and Georgia Amoore, the Mystics have shown that they are capable of beating any team on their day, and against the Dream, the Mystics have shown that they can contain Reese and Co. when needed, having won two of their three matchups this season.

However, Atlanta's 109-77 thrashing on June 6 is a testament to the Dream's capability when firing on all cylinders. They caught the Mystics off guard in that game, and that outing serves as a cautionary reminder of the Mystics' shortcomings.
